title: NT politician Yiŋiya Guyula resigns, labelling CLP policies 'dehumanising'

Topic:State and Territory Government

Yiŋiya Guyula has announced he will step down as the member for Mulka, effective immediately. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Independent Northern Territory MLA Yiŋiya Guyula has resigned as the member for Mulka, effective immediately.

In a statement, he said he could no longer "sit opposite a government who are not willing to listen or form partnerships" and labelled "too many" of the NT government's laws "dehumanising" and "oppressing".

Fellow politicians, including the federal Indigenous Australians minister, have paid tribute to Mr Guyula's time in parliament and advocacy for his community.

Member of the Northern Territory Legislative Assembly Yiŋiya Guyula has resigned effective immediately, citing in part the Country Liberal Party (CLP) government's introduction of legislation that is "dehumanising, oppressing and destroying" Aboriginal communities.

Mr Guyula was elected to the seat of Nhulunbuy, now known as Mulka, as an independent in 2016.

In a statement, Mr Guyula said the decision to step down had not been "easy", but that he felt it was necessary as he could no longer "sit opposite a government who are not willing to listen or form partnerships".

"I have been sent by my people to work with the government, but their answer has always been, 'we know what is best for you', rather than working in partnership with us," his statement read.

"What I have discovered is that Aboriginal communities are the political football that gets passed around with no real intention of working with our people to bring positive change for our communities."

Yiŋiya Guyula says he no longer feels he can sit opposite a government "who are not willing to listen". (ABC News: Peter Garnish)

Mr Guyula said the CLP government's recent passing of changes to child protection legislation had occurred with no consultation with remote communities.

"I appealed to the government to withdraw the bill and work with communities to bring real changes that will work," he said.

"Since their election, the CLP have introduced too many laws that are dehumanising, oppressing and destroying our communities and our people.

The independent member for Mulka — an electorate with a population of 9,500, mostly Yolŋu people — said the only way things would improve for Aboriginal people was if the government would "come and sit with us respectfully".

"We are kindly offering partnership, but instead of diplomacy, the government are walking all over us," he said.

In a social media post to his constituents, Mr Guyula said the Westminster system of government was also part of what was failing remote Aboriginal communities.

Yiŋiya Guyula says the NT government is "walking all over" Aboriginal people. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

"Government interest is focused on power and money rather than serving the people," he said.

"Many people are dying, and children have become involved in crime.

"This is not part of our culture; it is the result of a government that is walking all over us.

"They don't remember we are a sovereign nation."

Mr Guyula added he had been experiencing "health concerns" and wanted to "make space for someone else to come in with new energy to serve the electorate".

Despite that, he assured community members: "I will continue to serve the people as a Yolŋu leader for as long as I have left."

"I'm stepping out to support our leadership on country because we can see our children being taken away and I want to stand with everyone on country and do the work we need to do on country for our children and our people," he said.

"Bukmak, don't worry about me. I'm not leaving you.

"I am leaving the parliament to come closer to you to work together to look after each other through Yolŋu rom."

Yiŋiya Guyula has resigned saying he wants to "make space for someone else to come in with new energy to serve the electorate".  (ABC News: Ian Redfearn)

Mr Guyula thanked his electorate for their "hard work to make things better" and for choosing him as their representative.

"No-one thought a Yolŋu person could be elected as an independent member of parliament, but we did it three times," he wrote.

Mr Guyula's resignation comes exactly 10 years to the week since he beat Lynne Walker by eight votes to first win the seat of Nhulunbuy.

A by-election for the Northern Territory seat of Mulka has been set for September 12.

Born near Buckingham Bay in 1958, Mr Guyula grew up living a traditional life on his ancestral lands, constructing shelter from paperbark and hunting for bush tucker, and only learning English when he began attending school at age 10.

His first job was as a plane mechanic on Elcho Island, and he later trained as a pilot.

Yiŋiya Guyula was one of the first Yolŋu pilots in Australia. (Supplied)

Mr Guyula's political career began with controversy after he won his seat at the 2016 election by just eight votes.

The results were taken to the Court of Disputed Returns over allegations he had been ineligible to run.

In the case brought by the NT Electoral Commission, the agency said it had "received information" that Mr Guyula was a member of the Milingimbi Local Authority, one of nine local authorities that report to the regional council.

Yiŋiya Guyula won the East Arnhem Land seat in 2016 by under 10 votes. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

The law in the Northern Territory prevents someone who holds a public office from running in an election.

Ultimately, the presiding judge dismissed the case, finding the court process had not established Mr Guyula was in fact a member of the Milingimbi Local Authority.

In 2017, Mr Guyula proposed a bill of rights for Northern Territory residents based on the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous People.

Yiŋiya Guyula took his battle for treaty to the United Nations in New York City, in 2018. (ABC News: Matt Garrick)

However, the bill was ultimately labelled a failure after he accepted an amendment to it that said parliament would only consult further on greater statutory recognition for Indigenous people and "note" the fact that the UN's declaration existed.

Independent NT politician Yingiya Guyula says the $4 million already spent on the treaty process has been squandered.

As a long-term advocate for treaty, Mr Guyula spoke out in 2023 about the then-Territory Labor government's decision to end the work of its treaty commission and reject some of its key recommendations, which he felt was a waste of the $4 million spent on consultations.

In the lead-up to the 2024 election, which the CLP ultimately won, Mr Guyula also expressed concerns about the party's lack of support for a treaty.

Along with other NT crossbenchers, he has protested against the CLP government on issues of youth justice and child protection.

In a statement, the NT government thanked Mr Guyula for his service to the people of Mulka and to the NT parliament.

"Throughout his time in parliament, Yiŋiya has been a strong leader and advocate for his people, his culture and his country," the statement said.

"He has used his place in the Legislative Assembly to stand up for the communities he represents and to highlight the importance of language, lore and culture."

Members of the NT parliament crossbench, including Yiŋiya Guyula, protesting the government's youth justice policies in September last year. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

NT Labor MLA Chansey Paech said losing Mr Guyula's voice from parliament would be a big blow to the struggle to improve the lives of Indigenous people.

"I am incredibly proud of the role that Yiŋiya has done," Mr Paech said.

"He reminded Aboriginal people in Mulka that their voice mattered and that they mattered, and everything he did in parliament he did with passion, with conviction and with determination."

Federal Indigenous Australians Minister Malarndirri McCarthy said she had "much respect" for the member for Mulka.

"Yiŋiya Guyula is a man of great strength and leadership for his Mulka electorate, for the Yolŋu people and for the deeply held sense of justice he carried with him in the Northern Territory parliament," she said in a statement.

"I know his story is not done with his retirement.

"He will continue to fight for homelands, for justice and against racism."

Justine Davis says Yiŋiya Guyula was an influence in her own entry into politics.  (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

The independent member for Johnston, Justine Davis, credited Mr Guyula with her own entry into politics, and said while she understood his decision, she was "deeply saddened" by it.

"It's an incredible loss to our parliament, it's an incredible loss to the Territory," she said.

"He came in with generosity and with grace and with wisdom, and he reached out a hand and a hand was not met."

Ms Davis said Mr Guyula's departure, along with the resignation of Greens member Kat McNamara earlier this year, "says something very significant about the way this government is working and the way that people feel like they're being shut out".

"It's not limited to parliament. We saw the resignation of the children's commissioner, we saw the CEO of Danila Dilba stand down from the Tripartite Forum. These are people who are saying, 'We cannot work with this government,'" she said.

"The chief minister has said very explicitly, many times, 'If you don't agree with us, you can leave.' That's not a way to have good government."

Lidia Thorpe says Yiŋiya Guyula was a strong advocate for Yolŋu people in his 10 years in parliament.  (ABC: Patrick Stone)

Federal independent senator Lidia Thorpe said she was "heartbroken" to hear Mr Guyula had "made the difficult decision" to resign, calling him a "true representative for his people".

"For the past 10 years, he has worked his heart out to bring truth-telling and accountability to the NT parliament, and to stand up for Yolŋu people and justice for all people across the Territory," she said in a statement.

"His election as an Independent three times was historic. He showed that Aboriginal people can represent their communities on their own terms, accountable directly to their people rather than to any political party."

However, she backed Mr Guyula's criticisms of the NT government's laws and approach, saying, "I understand why he would make this decision."
